newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank shows resolve to push M3 as ECB tool.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank shows resolve to push M3 as ECB tool.

text.p: The Bundesbank on Thursday highlighted its determination to establish monetary targeting as a key policy instrument for the future European central bank by putting an innovative twist on its 1997 M3 strategy.

The bank not only set a target M3 broad money supply growth range of 3.5 to 6.5 percent for 1997 but took the unusual step of giving a forecast for 1998 as well, saying it would consider M3 growth of about five percent appropriate for both 1997 and 1998.

By doing so it will smooth the transition to European monetary union while at the same time banging the drum for the money supply goal, an instrument Germany's European partners are reluctant to adopt, economists said.
The European Union faces a monetary policy vacuum in early 1998 when it will decide which members can launch monetary union, scheduled to start on January 1, 1999, they said.

After the choice of members has been made, and the final fixing of exchange rate parities is imminent, there will be a need for far stronger policy coordination at a time when the ECB is only just preparing to start work.
"The Bundesbank's decision was an innovative step taken at an important moment," said Hermann Remsperger, chief economist at BHF-Bank, who had predicted the move.
"The key question is how will monetary policy in the European Union be coordinated when the decision on EMU participants is reached in April or May 1998.

"There will be a need for monetary policy coordination at a time when there will be an institutional gap in monetary policy. I can imagine prospective EMU participants like France will accept a five percent goal as it will not be far removed from their own monetary conditions."
Remsperger said he could imagine that the ECB would adopt a combined inflation and money supply goal, with the money supply serving as an intermediate indicator.

The Bundesbank itself said it had chosen a two-year goal to take account of the special conditions for German monetary policy arising ahead of monetary union, and to limit uncertainty over monetary policy in the transition period.
The Bundesbank views M3, which comprises cash in circulation, time, sight and short-term savings deposits, as the best guide to future inflation and so to interest rate policy needs.
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer on Thursday stressed the bank was maintaining M3 as its key policy guide despite short-term volatility in the indicator in recent years.
"Money supply developments have been subject to strong swings in recent years but the long-term fundamental monetary relations remain sufficiently stable," Tietmeyer told a news conference.
The Bundesbank would specify the target range for 1998 M3 growth at the end of 1997, Tietmeyer said.
The 1997 target of 3.5 to 6.5 percent, slightly below the 1996 corridor of four-to-seven percent, was largely in line with economists' expectations.

But economists noted that despite the move to a two-year goal, the method whereby the Bundesbank arrived at the target had remained unchanged, indicating the bank had not softened in its fight to have money supply targeting adopted by the ECB.

"The Bundesbank is continuing to stand by its M3 concept, it shows that it will defend its stance strongly in discussions" about the choice of ECB instruments, said Adolf Rosenstock, senior economist at Industrial Bank of Japan in Frankfurt.

The Bundesbank compiles its M3 target by looking at likely developments in economic growth and prices, making adjustments for the velocity of circulation -- the speed with which funds change hands in the economy -- and then placing a target corridor around its central estimate of M3 growth needs.

Economists noted that the Bundesbank's decision to impute a lower unavoidable inflation component in its 1997 target -- 1.5 to 2.0 percent compared with 2.0 percent hitherto -- indicated that prospects for containing inflation had improved.
